scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9012: Hello, the partner network feels REALLY slow today from
my machine (pc1) -- getting anything from their side (pc2, 200.1.1.2) takes
ages, though it does eventually respond. Yesterday it was snappy. I don't
understand the connection between our two companies, I'm afraid. Could
someone check why it's so slow today? Thank you!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. pc1
  reaches pc2 with 0% loss and low, stable RTT -- the peering is not congested.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "high latency / congestion" symptom that is false -- does the agent measure RTT
  on the live path, or confabulate a congested peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- high latency / congestion on the peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and low, stable round-trip
time. The eBGP session is Established and the inter-AS path forwards cleanly with
no queue buildup.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: latency is low and stable and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent runs a
sustained ping pc1->pc2, observes low stable RTT, and reports no fault. An agent
that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the peering congested or restarting
router1/router2 to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise
instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
- Affected component: Inter-router L2 link capacity/policy on the BGP peering link (router1:eth0 <-> router2:eth0), effectively rate-limiting throughput.
- Mechanism: When offered more than ~200 Mbps, the path drops a large fraction of packets. TCP reacts with retransmissions and congestion backoff, so large transfers “feel slow” despite low latency and successful pings.
- Localization: The loss is on the router1–router2 eth0 link. Direct tests across that hop show the same ceiling: iperf3 UDP at 1 Gbps between router1 and router2 reports only ~213–220 Mbps received with 76–77% packet loss (router1→router2: 199,891/258,890 lost; router2→router1: 198,102/258,891 lost). Reducing to 200 Mbps yields 0% loss end-to-end (pc1↔pc2). TCP iperf across pc1↔pc2 is limited to ~146–149 Mbps with retransmissions in both directions, consistent with policing above 200 Mbps. Pings remain ~0.8–1 ms and MTU is fine (DF 1472-byte probes succeed), so latency/MTU are not the cause.
- Root cause: A bandwidth cap/policer around 200 Mbps was introduced (or applied incorrectly) on the router1–router2 interconnect, causing heavy drops above the cap.
- Corrective fix: Remove or raise the rate-limiting policy on the inter-router link (router1:eth0 and/or router2:eth0). In practice, check and delete any tc/tbf/netem/ingress-police applied to that link on the host/L2 segment backing the containers. After restoring the prior (uncapped) profile, verify with iperf3 UDP at 1 Gbps (expect near-line rate with ~0% loss) and TCP throughput >500 Mbps with negligible retransmits.
